# Apples to Apples: Getting Type Mappings Right in LLM-Based Code Translation

What it takes for a type mapping between a source and target language to be correct — conversion soundness and round-trip preservation — and how Code Metal uses schema-based interface generators to build verified, behavior-preserving type mappings.

A major limitation of most LLM-based code translation systems is that they can generate code that compiles successfully without preserving the behavior of the source program. At Code Metal, we are addressing this challenge as we build systems for translating large and complex code bases across many source and target languages. In this post, we examine how choices about mapping types across languages contribute to this problem, what it takes for a mapping between source and target types to be correct, and how translation systems can meet that bar. Let’s begin with why choosing a target type is harder than it looks.

## What Makes a Type Mapping Correct

Deciding how types should map across languages is difficult because a choice made for one type affects how values flow through function bodies and across call sites. The right target type often depends not only on the source type itself, but also on how the program uses values of that type. A C function that takes a char * may use it to read text, write into a buffer, or access a sequence of raw bytes. Rust gives each of these uses a different type, and the C signature alone does not say which one is meant.

On the target language side, a type checker or compiler can validate that the generated code uses the chosen types consistently, but it cannot establish a correspondence between source and target values. A correctness claim about such a correspondence must begin by identifying the values for which conversion is expected to succeed. Some mappings may cover every value of the source type. Others may support only a subset and report an error for values outside it. A mapping from Python’s unbounded integers to C’s fixed-width integers, for example, cannot convert every source value.

To make this concept a little more precise, let σ be a source type in language S and τ a target type in language T , and write ⟦ σ ⟧ and ⟦ τ ⟧ for the sets of values admitted by those types. A value conversion function C S→T takes a value in ⟦ σ ⟧ and either returns ok(w) for some value w in the target language or reports an error. The value conversion function C T→S operates in the opposite direction. If σ is Python’s integer type and τ is C’s int , the value conversion function C Python→C returns the same integer when it fits in a C int and reports an error otherwise. The reverse value conversion function always succeeds because every C int has a corresponding Python integer.

The value conversion function in the opposite direction must satisfy the same property. Note that conversion soundness guarantees that a successful conversion produces a valid target value, but it does not guarantee that the value conversion function in the opposite direction recovers the original source value.

We say a mapping is lossless for a set of source values when converting any of those values to the target representation and back recovers the original source value. In our Python-to-C example, conversion is lossless for every Python integer that fits in a C int : converting the integer to C and then back to Python recovers the original value. Python integers outside that range cannot be converted to a C int , so they are not included in the set of values for which lossless conversion is promised.

A type mapping is correct when both value conversion functions are sound and the mapping is round-trip preserving on lossless S .

Both properties come into play when a source function is compared with the translated function on the same inputs. To compare a Python function with a C translation, a test harness has to convert every Python integer argument into a C int and convert every result back into Python. If these value conversion functions are sound but not round-trip preserving, an argument or result may change during conversion and introduce a disagreement between the two functions that is not a failure of the translation.

Now that we know what makes a type mapping correct, we need to figure out how to find one. The first step is choosing a target type for each occurrence of a source type, and the earlier char * example showed that this step is harder than it looks: the same C type can represent data used in several different ways, so the declared source type alone may not determine its Rust counterpart. We begin there.

## How a Program Uses Values Guides Type Translation

When the declared source type does not determine the target type, how the program uses values of that type can. We call this information program context . To see how context guides the choice of a target type, consider the following C function, adapted from Hong and Ryu’s paper on Tymcrat , an LLM-based tool for translating C programs into Rust. The function increments an integer through a pointer:

void inc ( int * p ) { * p += 1 ; }

A direct translation of the function inc maps the type of the C pointer p to the Rust raw pointer type *mut i32 . Dereferencing a raw pointer requires unsafe Rust, but the way the source C function uses p suggests a more idiomatic Rust type. Because inc reads and updates only a single integer at the address supplied by the caller, the type of p can be expressed in Rust as &mut i32 , a mutable reference to an integer:

fn inc ( p : & mut i32 ) { * p + = 1 ; }

The Rust compiler accepts this signature together with the translated body, but rejects one that declares p as an immutable reference, since the body writes through it.

Hong and Ryu built Tymcrat around the observation that choosing an idiomatic Rust signature can depend on how the source function uses its parameters. Before generating the body translation, Tymcrat uses the source function body to generate candidate Rust signatures and discards signatures containing type errors. It then generates a Rust function for each remaining signature, uses compiler feedback to reduce type errors, and selects a translation. This process happens in dependency order, so that the signature selected for each callee can be included in the prompt when generating callers.

Tymcrat reduced the number of type errors by 71.5 percent across 39 GNU programs, but Hong and Ryu emphasize that the absence of type errors does not establish correctness: their manual review found functions with no type errors whose translations did not preserve the original program behavior. These results show how program context can address one part of defining a type mapping: choosing target types that reflect how the source program uses values. The other part, showing that the chosen types make the mapping correct , remains open, since neither conversion soundness nor round-trip preservation follows from successful target compilation alone.

## Good Type Mappings Leave No Value Behind

Once a target type has been chosen, the next question is whether source values survive the trip into the target language and back. Two types may look equivalent, and code that uses them may compile, while the target type still fails to distinguish values that the source type keeps apart. When that happens, round-trip preservation is out of reach: two different source values are forced onto the same target value, and the reverse value conversion function cannot tell them apart any longer. The authors of Oxidizer , an LLM-based tool for translating Go programs into Rust, give a concrete example. Consider the following Go structure with a field of type []int :

type EntryDetail struct { Addenda05 [ ] int }

A plausible Rust translation gives the field Addenda05 the type Vec<i64> :

struct EntryDetail { addenda05 : Vec < i64 > , }

Both the types []int and Vec<i64> contain sequences of integers, but a Go []int value can be either nil or an empty sequence, while a Rust Vec<i64> value has only one empty representation. These two distinct Go values must therefore be mapped to the same Rust value. The Rust structure is well typed, and functions that use it may compile, but a value conversion function into Vec<i64> cannot be round-trip preserving for both Go values.

To detect this mismatch, Oxidizer introduces a notion of type compatibility . A target type is compatible with a source type when the source values being considered can be converted to the target type and back, with each round trip recovering the original source value. In the terminology of this post, a target type is compatible with a source type when there exists a type mapping between the two types that is lossless for a selected set of source values.

More concretely, Oxidizer instruments the source project and runs the project’s tests to collect input and output values for functions — i.e., the lossless S set of the mapping. Oxidizer then implements the two value conversion functions between Go and Rust through JSON. The value conversion function C Go→Rust serializes a Go value as JSON and deserializes the result into the proposed Rust type, and C Rust→Go serializes the Rust value and deserializes it back into Go. Using slightly abused notation, the recorded value v satisfies round-trip preservation when C Rust→Go ( C Go→Rust ( v )) = v .

In the example above, the nil value of type []int has no distinct counterpart in Vec<i64> : either C Go→Rust fails on it, or it produces the empty vector, which C Rust→Go maps back to an empty, non- nil sequence rather than to nil . Either way, round-trip preservation fails for that value. Because the recorded values come from the project test suite, Oxidizer establishes round-trip preservation only for values observed while running the tests. It does not explicitly define a type mapping or otherwise characterize the values for which the mapping is correct beyond those reached by the tests. To move beyond this limited guarantee, we need a type mapping whose supported values are specified independently of a project’s tests and whose correctness can be established for all of those values.

## Interface Generators to the Rescue

At Code Metal, we translate between many source and target languages, and we want to avoid writing, and proving, the same value conversion functions once for every pair of languages. A language-independent specification of values, shared by all languages, lets each language connect to the specification once instead of to every other language. Schema-based interface generators provide such a construction: they are commonly built around an interface definition language , or IDL, in which a schema describes structured values, paired with a serialization format that defines how the values described by that schema are represented as bytes. Together, the schema and the format form a language-independent specification of structured values and their valid serialized representations. A generator then produces language-specific data types, serializers, and deserializers that implement this specification.
